ECONOMIC ESPIONAGE ACT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Corp.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes the federal Economic Espionage Act, 18 U.S.C. §§ 1831–1839 -- specifically its two criminal offenses, 18 U.S.C. § 1831 (economic espionage benefiting a foreign government, instrumentality, or agent) and 18 U.S.C. § 1832 (theft of trade secrets generally, without any foreign-benefit element) -- what conduct each defines as a federal crime, the statutory definition of "trade secret" that applies to both offenses, and the penalties each statute specifies. It is prepared by Jane Doe concerning a situation involving Acme Corp. and, where relevant, John Smith. The trade secret information at issue is described as follows: customer pricing formulas. Both 18 U.S.C. § 1831 and § 1832 are federal criminal statutes: violations are investigated and prosecuted by federal law enforcement and the U.S. Department of Justice, not through a private lawsuit, and this document does not initiate, threaten, or request any criminal investigation or prosecution. It does not state that any specific conduct described above does or does not violate either statute, and it is not a substitute for that case-specific legal determination. This document is also distinct from, and does not replace, this project's existing Criminal Trade Secret Theft Information Sheet (California Penal Code section 499c, a separate state criminal statute) or this project's existing trade secret misappropriation documents describing the federal civil Defend Trade Secrets Act cause of action, 18 U.S.C. § 1836 -- a separate, non-criminal federal statute discussed further in a companion clause below.

THE FOREIGN-BENEFIT OFFENSE: 18 U.S.C. § 1831 (ECONOMIC ESPIONAGE)
18 U.S.C. § 1831 makes it a federal crime to steal, or without authorization appropriate, take, or obtain by fraud a trade secret; to copy, transmit, or otherwise convey a trade secret without authorization; to knowingly receive, buy, or possess a trade secret known to have been stolen; or to attempt or conspire to do any of those things -- but only where the person acts "intending or knowing that the offense will benefit any foreign government, foreign instrumentality, or foreign agent." This foreign-government-benefit element is what distinguishes section 1831 from section 1832, addressed in a companion clause, and it does not require that the foreign government itself direct or know of the conduct -- only that the person committing the offense intend or know that a foreign government, instrumentality, or agent will benefit. Except for organizations (addressed in a companion clause on organizational penalties), a violation of section 1831 is punishable by a fine of not more than $5,000,000, imprisonment of not more than 15 years, or both.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "(a) In General.—Whoever, intending or knowing that the offense will benefit any foreign government, foreign instrumentality, or foreign agent, knowingly— (1) steals, or without authorization appropriates, takes, carries away, or conceals, or by fraud, artifice, or deception obtains a trade secret; (2) without authorization copies, duplicates, sketches, draws, photographs, downloads, uploads, alters, destroys, photocopies, replicates, transmits, delivers, sends, mails, communicates, or conveys a trade secret; (3) receives, buys, or possesses a trade secret, knowing the same to have been stolen or appropriated, obtained, or converted without authorization; (4) attempts to commit any offense described in any of paragraphs (1) through (3); or (5) conspires with one or more other persons to commit any offense described in any of paragraphs (1) through (3), and one or more of such persons do any act to effect the object of the conspiracy, shall, except as provided in subsection (b), be fined not more than $5,000,000 or imprisoned not more than 15 years, or both."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1831(a) (Cornell LII text), Economic Espionage Act, foreign-benefit offense and individual penalty (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1831)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the full text of 18 U.S.C. § 1831(a), a single subsection consisting of an introductory clause, five numbered paragraphs describing the prohibited acts, and a closing penalty clause; it does not quote subsection (b) (the separate organizational penalty, addressed in a companion clause of this document) or the statutory definitions in section 1839 that give meaning to "trade secret," "foreign instrumentality," and "foreign agent" as used here (addressed in a companion clause). The $5,000,000 individual fine figure quoted above reflects a 2013 amendment (Pub. L. 112-269) that raised it from a prior $500,000 cap, per this section's own Cornell LII editorial notes, which this document did not independently verify against the amending Public Law's own text -- only against Cornell LII's summary of the amendment as fetched. This clause does not state that any specific conduct does or does not fall within section 1831, does not state that any specific defendant would or would not be found to have intended or known of a foreign-government benefit, and no case law construing section 1831 was researched or is cited here.

THE GENERAL OFFENSE: 18 U.S.C. § 1832 (THEFT OF TRADE SECRETS)
18 U.S.C. § 1832 separately makes it a federal crime to commit the same kind of acts described in section 1831 -- stealing, copying, receiving, attempting, or conspiring to obtain a trade secret without authorization -- but section 1832 does not require any intent or knowledge that a foreign government, instrumentality, or agent will benefit. Instead, section 1832 requires: intent to convert the trade secret to the economic benefit of someone other than its owner; that the trade secret be related to a product or service used in, or intended for use in, interstate or foreign commerce; and intent or knowledge that the offense will injure the trade secret's owner. Except for organizations (addressed in a companion clause), a violation of section 1832 is punishable by imprisonment of not more than 10 years -- five years less than the maximum for section 1831 -- and by a fine "under this title," rather than the specific $5,000,000 individual cap that section 1831 states by its own terms.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "(a) Whoever, with intent to convert a trade secret, that is related to a product or service used in or intended for use in interstate or foreign commerce, to the economic benefit of anyone other than the owner thereof, and intending or knowing that the offense will, injure any owner of that trade secret, knowingly— (1) steals, or without authorization appropriates, takes, carries away, or conceals, or by fraud, artifice, or deception obtains such information; (2) without authorization copies, duplicates, sketches, draws, photographs, downloads, uploads, alters, destroys, photocopies, replicates, transmits, delivers, sends, mails, communicates, or conveys such information; (3) receives, buys, or possesses such information, knowing the same to have been stolen or appropriated, obtained, or converted without authorization; (4) attempts to commit any offense described in paragraphs (1) through (3); or (5) conspires with one or more other persons to commit any offense described in paragraphs (1) through (3), and one or more of such persons do any act to effect the object of the conspiracy, shall, except as provided in subsection (b), be fined under this title or imprisoned not more than 10 years, or both."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1832(a) (Cornell LII text), Economic Espionage Act, general trade secret theft offense and individual penalty (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1832)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the full text of 18 U.S.C. § 1832(a), a single subsection with the same five-paragraph structure as section 1831(a); it does not quote subsection (b) (the organizational penalty, addressed in a companion clause). The phrase "fined under this title" is quoted directly from the statute as fetched; this document does not independently trace or quote the general federal fine statute that phrase cross-references (18 U.S.C. § 3571, which sets default fine ceilings for federal offenses generally, including alternative fines tied to gain or loss in some cases), because section 3571 was not fetched or verified as part of this research -- a reader wanting the actual individual dollar exposure for a section 1832 violation would need to separately research section 3571. This document's initial working assumption, before this statutory text was fetched, was that section 1831 and section 1832 stated the same specific individual fine figure; that assumption is corrected here: only section 1831 states a specific individual dollar cap in its own text, and section 1832 does not. This clause does not state that any specific conduct does or does not fall within section 1832, and no case law construing section 1832 was researched or is cited here.

ORGANIZATIONAL PENALTIES DIFFER BETWEEN THE TWO OFFENSES
Both 18 U.S.C. § 1831 and § 1832 state a separate, higher-ceiling penalty for an organization (rather than an individual) that commits the offense. Under section 1831(b), an organization that commits the foreign-benefit offense is subject to a fine of not more than the greater of $10,000,000 or three times the value of the stolen trade secret to the organization, including research-and-design and other reproduction costs the organization avoided by the theft. Under section 1832(b), an organization that commits the general offense is subject to a fine of not more than the greater of $5,000,000 or that same three-times-value measure. The $10,000,000 organizational floor for section 1831 is twice the $5,000,000 organizational floor for section 1832, mirroring the two offenses' different individual-penalty severity.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "(b) Organizations.— Any organization that commits any offense described in subsection (a) shall be fined not more than the greater of $10,000,000 or 3 times the value of the stolen trade secret to the organization, including expenses for research and design and other costs of reproducing the trade secret that the organization has thereby avoided."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1831(b) (Cornell LII text), Economic Espionage Act, organizational penalty for the foreign-benefit offense (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1831)
  "(b) Any organization that commits any offense described in subsection (a) shall be fined not more than the greater of $5,000,000 or 3 times the value of the stolen trade secret to the organization, including expenses for research and design and other costs of reproducing the trade secret that the organization has thereby avoided."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1832(b) (Cornell LII text), Economic Espionage Act, organizational penalty for the general offense (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1832)
  Known gap: This clause cites two different statutory sections' organizational-penalty subsections -- 18 U.S.C. § 1831(b) and § 1832(b) -- which are independent provisions of independent sections, not subdivisions of one section, grouped here only because both describe the same kind of organizational fine. Per each section's own Cornell LII editorial notes (not independently verified against the amending Public Laws' own text), the "greater of [amount] or 3 times the value" formulation was added to section 1831(b) by a 2013 amendment (replacing a flat $10,000,000 cap) and to section 1832(b) by a 2016 amendment (replacing a flat $5,000,000 cap); this document does not further trace either amendment's legislative history. This clause does not address how "the value of the stolen trade secret to the organization" is calculated or proven in any specific case, and no case law construing either organizational-penalty subsection was researched or is cited here.

THE STATUTORY DEFINITION OF "TRADE SECRET" GOVERNING BOTH OFFENSES
18 U.S.C. § 1839(3) defines "trade secret," for purposes of this entire chapter of the federal criminal code (Chapter 90 of Title 18, which contains sections 1831 through 1839), as all forms and types of financial, business, scientific, technical, economic, or engineering information -- regardless of how it is stored or memorialized -- if its owner has taken reasonable measures to keep it secret and it derives independent economic value from not being generally known to, or readily ascertainable by, others who could profit from disclosing or using it. Because section 1839 defines this term for the chapter as a whole rather than separately within section 1831 or section 1832, the identical statutory text governs the "trade secret" element of both federal criminal offenses described in this document. That same section 1839 definition also governs the federal civil cause of action for trade secret misappropriation under 18 U.S.C. § 1836, discussed in a companion clause and elsewhere in this project's confidentiality-agreement documents -- so the criminal and civil definitions are not merely similar, as California's separate criminal (Penal Code section 499c) and civil (CUTSA) trade secret definitions are; they are the same statutory text, because Congress placed sections 1831 (criminal), 1832 (criminal), 1836 (civil), and 1839 (definitions) in the same chapter and had section 1839 apply chapter-wide.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "(3) the term “trade secret” means all forms and types of financial, business, scientific, technical, economic, or engineering information, including patterns, plans, compilations, program devices, formulas, designs, prototypes, methods, techniques, processes, procedures, programs, or codes, whether tangible or intangible, and whether or how stored, compiled, or memorialized physically, electronically, graphically, photographically, or in writing if— (A) the owner thereof has taken reasonable measures to keep such information secret; and (B) the information derives independent economic value, actual or potential, from not being generally known to, and not being readily ascertainable through proper means by, another person who can obtain economic value from the disclosure or use of the information;"
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1839(3) (Cornell LII text), Economic Espionage Act, definition of "trade secret" applicable chapter-wide (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1839)
  Known gap: This clause quotes 18 U.S.C. § 1839(3), one paragraph of a single statutory section that also separately defines "foreign instrumentality," "foreign agent," "owner," "misappropriation," "improper means," and "Trademark Act of 1946" in its other paragraphs, none of which are requoted here. The observation that section 1839's definition governs section 1836 as well as sections 1831 and 1832 is based on this section's own introductory phrase, "As used in this chapter," and this researcher's confirmation that sections 1831, 1832, 1836, and 1839 are all part of the same chapter (Chapter 90 of Title 18) as fetched from Cornell LII's own breadcrumb navigation on each page; it is not a holding from any case construing that structural point, and no case law is cited here. This document does not independently verify that this exact text is the version currently in force by any means other than the Cornell LII page fetched on the date below; Cornell LII states this paragraph was last amended in 2016.

HOW THIS FEDERAL CRIMINAL STATUTE RELATES TO STATE CRIMINAL LAW AND FEDERAL CIVIL LAW
18 U.S.C. §§ 1831 and 1832 are federal crimes, investigated and prosecuted by federal authorities. They are legally distinct from two other trade-secret-related mechanisms addressed elsewhere in this project: (1) California Penal Code section 499c, a separate state criminal statute prosecuted by California district attorneys or the California Attorney General, addressed in this project's own Criminal Trade Secret Theft Information Sheet; and (2) the federal civil cause of action for trade secret misappropriation under 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b), which a private trade secret owner -- not a prosecutor -- may bring in federal court, addressed in this project's trade secret misappropriation and NDA documents. Section 1836 is not solely private, either: section 1836(a) separately authorizes the U.S. Attorney General to bring a civil action for injunctive relief against a violation of this chapter, a third, non-criminal, non-private federal mechanism distinct from both a private section 1836(b) lawsuit and a section 1831/1832 criminal prosecution. The Economic Espionage Act's own construction provision, 18 U.S.C. § 1838, states that -- apart from one whistleblower-notice-related exception -- the chapter is not to be construed to preempt or displace other civil or criminal remedies provided by federal, state, or territorial law for trade secret misappropriation, meaning this federal criminal statute, a state Penal Code section 499c prosecution, and a federal or state civil suit over the same underlying conduct are not mutually exclusive as a matter of the statute's own text.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "Except as provided in section 1833(b), this chapter shall not be construed to preempt or displace any other remedies, whether civil or criminal, provided by United States Federal, State, commonwealth, possession, or territory law for the misappropriation of a trade secret, or to affect the otherwise lawful disclosure of information by any Government employee under section 552 of title 5 (commonly known as the Freedom of Information Act)."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1838 (Cornell LII text), Economic Espionage Act, construction with other civil and criminal remedies (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1838)
  "The Attorney General may, in a civil action, obtain appropriate injunctive relief against any violation of this chapter."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1836(a) (Cornell LII text), Economic Espionage Act, Attorney General civil action for injunctive relief (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1836)
  Known gap: This clause cites two separate statutory sections -- 18 U.S.C. § 1838 (a single section) and 18 U.S.C. § 1836(a) (one subsection of a different section already partly addressed, as to its private-suit subsection (b), by other clauses in this project's separate trade secret misappropriation documents) -- grouped together here only because both illustrate that sections 1831/1832 do not occupy the field. This clause does not address whether, or how, a single set of underlying facts that supports a federal section 1831 or 1832 prosecution could also support a Penal Code section 499c prosecution, a private section 1836(b) civil suit, or an Attorney General section 1836(a) civil action, or how such proceedings might interact procedurally (for example, as to timing, double jeopardy, parallel discovery, or use of evidence from one proceeding in another) -- none of which is addressed by the statutory text quoted here or elsewhere researched for this document. The reference above to a "whistleblower-notice-related exception" describes section 1838's own cross-reference to section 1833(b) exactly as fetched; section 1833(b) itself is not requoted in this document (it is quoted elsewhere in this project's trade secret misappropriation documents). No case law construing section 1838 or section 1836(a) was researched or is cited here.

CLOSING NOTICE
This Information Sheet regarding the federal Economic Espionage Act, 18 U.S.C. §§ 1831–1839, concerning Acme Corp. and, where relevant, John Smith, states federal law as fetched and verified on the date below. It is a general reference describing what these federal criminal statutes say; it is not a report to law enforcement, not a request for a criminal investigation or prosecution, and not a determination that any specific conduct described in this Information Sheet does or does not violate 18 U.S.C. § 1831, § 1832, or any other statute. A decision about whether to report suspected conduct to federal law enforcement, a United States Attorney's office, or any other authority is a separate decision this document does not make and does not recommend.

Prepared by: Jane Doe

Date: January 1, 2026

City, state: Los Angeles, California

The Economic Espionage Act's own construction provision, 18 U.S.C. § 1838, states that -- apart from one whistleblower-notice-related exception -- the chapter is not to be construed to preempt or displace other civil or criminal remedies provided by federal, state, or territorial law for trade secret misappropriation, meaning this federal criminal statute, a state Penal Code section 499c prosecution, and a federal or state civil suit over the same underlying conduct are not mutually exclusive as a matter of the statute's own text.
